global.title: Note citations give generated answers an inspectable evidence trail.
global.content:
An answer is easier to audit when its supporting records are identifiable and accessible. The guide states: "An answer that cites the notes it used can be checked by opening them" and contrasts this with an answer from a model's general knowledge.
The advantage is traceability, not guaranteed correctness: a cited note may be wrong or may fail to support the answer. Where the notes can be opened, citations let a reader check that relationship directly rather than infer the model's basis.
global.description: Opening the referenced notes lets a reader test an answer's support instead of relying on unexposed model knowledge.

global.title: Knowledge Vault preserves contradictory claims as an unresolved tension.
global.content:
When notes disagree, Knowledge Vault records the dispute rather than making the collection look consistent by removing one position. The tension names the competing notes so subsequent evidence can address the disagreement explicitly.
The source says: "the vault opens a tension that names both, so the disagreement stays visible until new evidence decides it, or shows that each claim holds under different conditions."
This applies to contradictory notes; retaining both does not imply that both are true. It predicts a visible unresolved issue until evidence supports a resolution or a distinction in scope.
global.description: Both positions remain visible while evidence may resolve the dispute or reveal that they apply under different conditions.

lifecycleEvents.comment: Extracted from "How Knowledge Vault works" (Links and maps of your topics, paragraph 3) by gpt-6.1-sol. Check the claim, its type and topics, then approve.

global.title: Linked retirement preserves the reasoning trail when knowledge changes.
global.content:
When a claim is superseded, retain the old note as an archive and explicitly connect its replacement. The guide explains that "linking it as the replacement and archiving the older note keeps the history".
Deletion removes the earlier position, while an unlinked archive can leave the reason for retirement unclear. This pattern applies when one note actually replaces another; unresolved disagreement should not be mistaken for supersession. It lets a reader reconstruct what changed rather than seeing only the latest belief.
global.description: Keeping the superseded note and identifying its successor records both the earlier position and the direction of revision.

global.title: A note with a single claim gives incoming links an unambiguous target.
global.content:
A link points to a note as a whole. If the destination contains several independent ideas, the reader must infer which idea motivated the connection; separating those ideas removes that ambiguity.
The source states: "A note that holds one idea can be linked precisely; a note that holds several can only be linked vaguely."
This applies when links address whole notes rather than specific passages. It predicts that splitting a mixed note into independently meaningful claims will make its incoming connections easier to interpret, though their rationales still need explanation.
global.description: Readers can follow a connection without first deciding which part of the destination is relevant.

global.title: An explicit rationale makes a connection between notes interpretable and checkable.
global.content:
A bare connection identifies two endpoints but leaves their relationship unspecified. A rationale supplies the missing proposition, allowing a reader to judge whether the connection is warranted.
The source states: "A link between two notes is useful only when it says why they connect." It contrasts an explained extension of a claim with "a bare line between two notes" that cannot be checked in the same way.
This concerns links used to communicate reasoning, rather than merely record adjacency. It predicts that a dense graph without explanations can still leave readers unable to understand why its notes belong together.
global.description: Explaining the relationship turns a bare association into a proposition that readers can evaluate.

global.title: Knowledge Vault provides a central map that opens access to its thematic maps.
global.content:
Knowledge Vault places a vault-wide entry point above its thematic maps. This separates choosing an area to explore from navigating the notes within that area.
The source specifies: "one map at the top, named after the vault, leads to all the others."
This describes access to the map collection, not a requirement that every note link directly from the top map. It predicts that a reader starting at the vault-named map can reach the thematic maps without already knowing their individual names.
global.description: The entry map is named after the vault, giving readers a stable starting point without requiring a topic to be chosen in advance.

global.title: My Vault
global.description: The vault's entry point: every domain and topic map hangs from here.
global.orientation: Start here. Each map below collects the notes on one theme; open the one closest to your question.

global.title: Claim-based titles let notes participate directly in reasoning.
global.content:
An argumentative title exposes what the note asks a reader to accept. That makes it possible to assess the note's role in an argument before opening it, rather than treating it only as material filed under a subject.
The source explains: "A claim can be used in an argument and someone can disagree with it; a topic label can only be filed under something."
This distinction concerns notes intended to express ideas, not navigation labels whose purpose is classification. It predicts that claim-based titles will make support and disagreement easier to identify than titles that name only a topic.
global.description: An assertion can be supported, challenged, or used as a premise; a category name leaves the actual position unstated.

global.title: Chat edits become persistent only through an explicit user application step.
global.content:
Knowledge Vault separates proposing a change from committing it. Chat may offer to save an answer or alter project work, but "it shows each change first, and nothing is written until you apply it."
The workflow is proposal, preview, then user application. Merely discussing or receiving a suggested edit should not modify stored work. This safeguard applies to chat-proposed changes and does not describe every other write path in the application.
global.description: Proposed note saves and project changes are shown before commitment, separating conversational suggestions from writes.

global.title: Hosted inference moves the source-processing boundary to an external provider.
global.content:
A hosted model needs access to its input outside the user's machine. The guide explicitly says that "the text being processed is sent to that provider".
The transfer concerns the text submitted for processing; it does not establish that every vault record is uploaded. Selecting hosting therefore changes the disclosure boundary for source processing and must not be treated as merely a speed setting.
global.description: Choosing a remote model entails transferring the text it needs, even though the vault's persistent records remain local by default.

global.title: Local inference avoids hosted model usage charges.
global.content:
The guide presents local processing as having no model-running charge: a local model "costs nothing to run". The relevant distinction is between using local compute and consuming a hosted model service.
This is a stated cost property, not a demonstrated total-cost analysis. Hardware, electricity, and maintenance costs are not assessed. The claim supports expecting no hosted inference bill from the local processing step, not assuming that operating a computer is literally free.
global.description: Processing uses the user's machine rather than a billed provider endpoint; the guide does not account for hardware or electricity.

global.title: Knowledge Vault records a rationale alongside every connection it draws.
global.content:
Knowledge Vault represents a generated connection as more than a pair of endpoints: it also carries an explanation of why the notes belong in that relationship.
The source specifies: "Each link the vault draws between two notes carries its reason."
This is a documented property of vault-created links, not evidence that every explanation is correct or that externally created links follow the same rule. It predicts that inspecting a generated connection should reveal a rationale available for review.
global.description: Generated links expose their justification so readers can inspect more than the identities of the connected notes.

global.title: Knowledge Vault’s knowledge lifecycle
global.description: How Knowledge Vault turns sources into atomic claims, connects and organizes them, and supports review, retrieval, and revision. Covers the processing choices and privacy boundaries governing that lifecycle.
global.orientation: Start with why a note should express one claim, then follow source capture and processing through linking, thematic navigation, and user approval. Read retrieval and retirement next; together, the notes argue that useful automated knowledge management requires inspectable reasoning, preserved history, and explicit user control, including control over external processing.

global.title: Consolidating equivalent claims makes their combined support easier to see.
global.content:
When several sources assert the same idea, separate notes divide the surrounding evidence network. A consolidated note gives readers one place to inspect the support accumulated across sources.
The source explains that duplicates, "kept apart, ... split the links between them, so neither shows how much support the idea really has."
Consolidation fits genuinely equivalent assertions. Claims with different conditions or incompatible implications should remain distinguishable rather than being flattened into apparent agreement. Where equivalence holds, consolidation predicts a more complete visible account of support, not necessarily stronger or more independent evidence.
global.description: A shared note concentrates supporting connections that would otherwise be scattered across duplicate destinations.

global.title: Semantic retrieval bridges differences between a question's wording and a note's phrasing.
global.content:
Meaning-based search compares conceptual relevance rather than relying only on shared words. The guide illustrates this with "why do my links feel vague" finding a note about one idea per note, explaining that "the vault compares meanings".
This supports retrieval when a question describes the consequence of an idea instead of naming it. It does not guarantee success for every paraphrase or ambiguous query, but predicts useful matches even when exact wording differs.
global.description: Queries can express a symptom or implication rather than repeat a note's vocabulary and still retrieve the relevant idea.

global.title: Search meaning representations are computed inside the user's machine.
global.content:
The semantic computation used by Knowledge Vault search is local. The guide describes "meanings that are computed on this computer" as the basis for comparison.
This places representation generation within the device boundary. It does not establish where every other AI operation runs: source processing can separately use a hosted model. A hosted processing choice therefore should not be assumed to relocate search representation computation.
global.description: Semantic search does not require an external service to create the representations used for meaning comparison.

global.title: Duplicating a searchable source passage contributes no distinct retrieval value.
global.content:
If searching the retained source already retrieves a passage, placing that passage in a separate note does not add otherwise unavailable information. The derived note needs a contribution beyond reproduction to justify itself as a retrieval object.
The source states: "The source stays in the vault as the record, so a note that only repeats a passage adds nothing that searching the source would not find."
The claim depends on the source remaining searchable and the note doing nothing more than repeating it. It does not cover a note that adds interpretation or useful connections. It predicts little retrieval benefit from creating bare excerpt notes under those conditions.
global.description: When the original remains available, a useful derived note must contribute something beyond another copy of the same text.

global.title: Local model processing keeps source text within the user's computer.
global.content:
Choosing a local model places inference alongside the source text rather than at a remote provider. The guide states: "A model on this computer keeps everything on the machine".
This describes the model-processing path, not every possible external connection. A separately configured converter or shared server can introduce another transfer path. Local inference therefore predicts no provider upload for that processing step, not universal network isolation.
global.description: The inference boundary stays on the device, avoiding the provider transfer required by hosted processing.

global.title: Independent processing stages allow recovery without replaying completed work.
global.content:
Knowledge Vault divides source processing into extracting ideas, connecting notes, placing them in thematic maps, and verifying the result. Separating these responsibilities makes a failure local to a stage rather than forcing the entire pipeline to restart.
The source explains: "Because each step stands on its own, a step that fails can be run again without redoing the steps before it."
The benefit depends on earlier results remaining available and valid for the retry. It predicts that a verification failure, for example, need not require extracting the source's ideas again; it does not establish that every downstream result remains valid after an earlier stage changes.
global.description: Extraction, linking, map placement, and verification form separate retry boundaries for source processing.

global.title: Model selection changes future processing rather than revising stored notes.
global.content:
Knowledge Vault separates the model used to produce notes from the notes already persisted. The guide states: "Switching models changes how new sources are processed; notes already written stay as they are."
A model switch alone should therefore leave existing note wording intact. Future outputs may differ, but updating earlier notes requires a separate action rather than occurring as a side effect of changing models.
global.description: Existing notes remain stable across a model switch, so changing inference providers is not a migration or regeneration operation.

global.title: Hosted inference favors processing speed over local execution in Knowledge Vault.
global.content:
The guide contrasts local execution, which "is slower", with the statement "A hosted model is faster". It also describes processing "one source at a time" locally and "a few at once" with hosting.
Within the documented setup, hosting should shorten processing waits and accommodate more simultaneous sources. No model specifications or benchmark results are supplied, so this comparison is not a universal performance ranking for all hardware and providers.
global.description: The guide pairs faster hosted processing with greater concurrency, making hosting the throughput-oriented option.

global.title: How Knowledge Vault works
global.content:
# How Knowledge Vault works

Knowledge Vault turns the documents you collect into a network of short notes. Each note holds one idea and is linked to the notes it supports, extends or contradicts. This guide is a source like any other: the notes written from it explain how the vault works, so reading them is a tour of how it thinks.

## Notes that hold one idea

A note that holds one idea can be linked precisely; a note that holds several can only be linked vaguely. A link to a note that mixes three ideas says that something in it is relevant, and whoever follows it has to work out which part. One idea per note is what lets each link carry a meaning.

A note's title states its idea as a claim, such as "One idea per note makes links precise", not a topic such as "Note-taking". A claim can be used in an argument and someone can disagree with it; a topic label can only be filed under something.

Restating an idea in new words, rather than copying the passage, is what tests whether it was understood. The source stays in the vault as the record, so a note that only repeats a passage adds nothing that searching the source would not find.

Two sources that make the same point are worth more as one note than as two: kept apart, the duplicates split the links between them, so neither shows how much support the idea really has.

## Links and maps of your topics

A link between two notes is useful only when it says why they connect. "This note builds on that one because it extends the claim from teams to individuals" can be checked by a reader; a bare line between two notes cannot. Each link the vault draws between two notes carries its reason.

A link also has a kind: one note can build on another, contradict it, replace it, or relate to it. The kind tells you how to read a pair of notes before you open either of them.

Contradictions are kept rather than settled by deleting one side. When two notes contradict each other, the vault opens a tension that names both, so the disagreement stays visible until new evidence decides it, or shows that each claim holds under different conditions.

Maps of your topics keep a growing vault navigable. Each map gathers the notes on one theme and points to the maps next to it, and one map at the top, named after the vault, leads to all the others. A map is only made once a theme has three or more notes, so a small vault is not cluttered with near-empty maps.

## How a source becomes notes

A source is processed in four steps: extract its ideas as notes, connect them to the notes already in the vault, place them in the maps of your topics, and verify the result. Because each step stands on its own, a step that fails can be run again without redoing the steps before it.

Adding a source should take seconds even though reading it takes minutes: a vault fills only while collecting stays effortless, so processing runs in the background while you keep working: one source at a time with a model on this computer, a few at once with a hosted one.

The AI model you choose decides how fast processing is and where your text goes. A model on this computer keeps everything on the machine and costs nothing to run, but it is slower. A hosted model is faster, and the text being processed is sent to that provider. Switching models changes how new sources are processed; notes already written stay as they are.

A new note waits in review until you approve it. The verify step reports which notes are ready to approve and which need a closer look, and approving a note makes it the vault's settled view.

Knowledge is better retired than deleted. When a newer note replaces an older one, linking it as the replacement and archiving the older note keeps the history: the archived note leaves search, but you can still see what was believed before and why it changed.

## Asking your vault

An answer that cites the notes it used can be checked by opening them; an answer from a model's general knowledge cannot be. That is why the vault's chat answers from your notes and names them.

A chat that cannot change anything on its own can be trusted with the vault. It can offer to save an answer as a note or to change the work in your projects, but it shows each change first, and nothing is written until you apply it.

Search finds notes by meaning, not only by matching words. A question phrased differently from the note, such as "why do my links feel vague" for the note about one idea per note, still finds it, because the vault compares meanings that are computed on this computer.

A vault stays on this computer unless you connect it to something else: a hosted AI model, a converter on another machine, or a vault shared on a server. Your sources, notes and links are stored locally, and nothing you add is sent anywhere by default.

global.title: A minimum note threshold prevents premature thematic maps from cluttering a vault.
global.content:
Creating a map for every emerging theme would add navigation overhead before there is enough material to organize. Knowledge Vault instead delays map creation until the theme contains at least three notes.
The source states: "A map is only made once a theme has three or more notes, so a small vault is not cluttered with near-empty maps."
The threshold governs map creation, not whether an isolated note is worth retaining. It predicts that themes with one or two notes will not yet receive maps; reaching three satisfies the minimum but does not, by itself, establish that a map must immediately be created.
global.description: Knowledge Vault waits for at least three notes on a theme before creating its map, avoiding navigation objects with little content.

lifecycleEvents.comment: Extracted from "How Knowledge Vault works" (Links and maps of your topics, paragraph 4) by gpt-6.1-sol. Check the claim, its type and topics, then approve.

global.title: Archiving separates historical access from active search results.
global.content:
Knowledge Vault treats archival retention and search visibility as separate concerns. The guide states: "the archived note leaves search, but you can still see what was believed before and why it changed."
An archived note is therefore not deleted, but ordinary search should no longer surface it as active knowledge. This supports cleaner retrieval while preserving historical inspection; it does not mean archived material remains searchable through the normal search path.
global.description: Retired claims stop competing with current knowledge during retrieval without losing their value as records of earlier belief.

global.title: Relationship labels preview how linked claims should be read together.
global.content:
Different connections call for different readings: a contradiction invites comparison, while a replacement signals that an earlier claim has been superseded. A relationship label supplies that orientation before the full arguments are inspected.
The source says: "The kind tells you how to read a pair of notes before you open either of them."
A type previews the relationship but does not establish its correctness or explain all its details. It predicts that typed links will help readers choose what to inspect and how to approach it, while rationales and note content remain necessary for evaluation.
global.description: Distinguishing extension, contradiction, replacement, and association gives readers an interpretive frame before opening either note.

lifecycleEvents.comment: Extracted from "How Knowledge Vault works" (Links and maps of your topics, paragraph 2) by gpt-6.1-sol. Check the claim, its type and topics, then approve.

global.title: Reconstructing an idea in new language exposes whether it was understood.
global.content:
Writing an idea afresh requires distinguishing its meaning from the sentence that originally expressed it. Copying can bypass that work, leaving apparent comprehension untested.
The source says: "Restating an idea in new words, rather than copying the passage, is what tests whether it was understood."
This applies to conceptual reconstruction, not cosmetic substitutions of individual words. Rephrasing is a test rather than a guarantee of correctness: difficulty restating an idea predicts a need to revisit the source, while a fluent restatement still needs checking for fidelity.
global.description: Copying preserves the author's wording without requiring the writer to recover the underlying meaning.

lifecycleEvents.comment: Extracted from "How Knowledge Vault works" (Notes that hold one idea, paragraph 3) by gpt-6.1-sol. Check the claim, its type and topics, then approve.

global.title: External data transfer is opt-in for a locally stored Knowledge Vault.
global.content:
Knowledge Vault's default storage and transfer boundary is the user's computer. The guide states: "Your sources, notes and links are stored locally, and nothing you add is sent anywhere by default."
The stated exceptions are connections to a hosted AI model, a converter on another machine, or a vault shared on a server. Without such configuration, adding content should not transmit it externally. Local storage alone does not imply no disclosure once an external integration is enabled.
global.description: Hosted models, remote converters, and shared servers are exceptions to the default device boundary, not prerequisites for storing knowledge.

lifecycleEvents.comment: Extracted from "How Knowledge Vault works" (Asking your vault, paragraph 4) by gpt-6.1-sol. Check the claim, its type and topics, then approve.

global.title: Connected thematic maps provide navigable routes through a growing note collection.
global.content:
Thematic maps reduce the need to confront the collection as an undifferentiated set. Each map offers a local view of a subject, while links to neighboring maps provide routes beyond that local view.
The source explains: "Maps of your topics keep a growing vault navigable. Each map gathers the notes on one theme and points to the maps next to it".
This approach depends on maps reflecting useful themes and maintaining meaningful neighboring connections; the source does not establish a scale at which navigation is guaranteed. It predicts that adding notes need not make discovery depend entirely on remembering individual titles.
global.description: Grouping notes by theme and linking neighboring maps supports movement both within a subject and across related subjects.

lifecycleEvents.comment: Extracted from "How Knowledge Vault works" (Links and maps of your topics, paragraph 4) by gpt-6.1-sol. Check the claim, its type and topics, then approve.

global.title: Verification directs review attention according to a note's readiness for approval.
global.content:
Verification acts as review triage rather than as automatic acceptance. The guide says it "reports which notes are ready to approve and which need a closer look".
This gives the reviewer a way to distinguish apparently ready candidates from those needing more scrutiny. A readiness report does not itself approve a note, nor does the source specify the checks used to produce that report.
global.description: The final processing stage flags candidates needing closer examination while leaving the approval decision with the user.

lifecycleEvents.comment: Extracted from "How Knowledge Vault works" (How a source becomes notes, paragraph 4) by gpt-6.1-sol. Check the claim, its type and topics, then approve.

global.title: User approval gives a generated note the status of accepted knowledge.
global.content:
A generated note is provisional until a person accepts it. The guide says, "A new note waits in review until you approve it" and "approving a note makes it the vault's settled view."
This separates producing a plausible claim from endorsing it. Successful generation or verification alone does not settle the vault's position; an unapproved note should remain pending rather than acquire accepted status automatically.
global.description: Generation produces a review candidate, not an endorsed position; the user controls the transition between those states.

lifecycleEvents.comment: Extracted from "How Knowledge Vault works" (How a source becomes notes, paragraph 4) by gpt-6.1-sol. Check the claim, its type and topics, then approve.

global.title: Background processing separates source submission time from analysis time.
global.content:
Knowledge Vault moves processing outside the immediate submission interaction. This allows acknowledging a source quickly while the more time-consuming reading and transformation continue separately.
The source says: "Adding a source should take seconds even though reading it takes minutes" and "processing runs in the background while you keep working".
This separation improves the responsiveness of capture, not necessarily the time until notes are ready. It predicts that slow analysis can coexist with quick submission, while queued work may still delay completed results.
global.description: Users can return to their work after capture instead of waiting for document processing to finish.

global.title: Knowledge Vault uses different source concurrency policies for local and hosted models.
global.content:
The selected model location determines how many sources Knowledge Vault processes simultaneously. The local path serializes sources; the hosted path permits limited parallel processing.
The source specifies: "one source at a time with a model on this computer, a few at once with a hosted one."
This is the vault's documented scheduling behavior, not a universal limitation of local models or a promise of unlimited hosted capacity. It predicts that a local batch progresses source by source, whereas a hosted batch can have several sources in progress together.
global.description: Local processing handles one source at a time, while hosted processing allows a few sources to run concurrently.

global.title: Low-friction source collection is a prerequisite for continued vault growth.
global.content:
A vault can develop only from material that people actually submit. Repeated effort at the point of collection threatens that input stream, making capture friction a constraint on continued accumulation.
The source expresses the dependency directly: "a vault fills only while collecting stays effortless".
This concerns growth through ongoing source collection, not the quality of existing notes. Low friction is presented as necessary, not sufficient: it cannot ensure that sources are useful or processed well. It predicts that burdensome submission will undermine continued collection even if downstream analysis is strong.
global.description: If collecting material becomes burdensome, fewer sources enter the system regardless of how capable later processing may be.
